A pattern I keep seeing: agent demos look good in the first week. The hard part starts later, when the agent meets real data, real permissions and real users.

An agent is a model working inside a system. When it fails, the cause can sit in the model, in the context it was given, in its tools, in the workflow around it, or in the check that should have caught the mistake. Each of those has a different fix and a different owner, and most of this post is about telling them apart.

Across model generations, the model decides what is possible. SWE-bench scores went from under 5% when the benchmark launched in late 2023 to over 80% by late 2025, on the cleaned-up [Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) subset, and no amount of prompt polish would have closed that gap. Within the current top tier the balance flips. LangChain moved its coding agent from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by [changing only the harness](https://www.langchain.com/blog/improving-deep-agents-with-harness-engineering) around a fixed model. The model sets the ceiling, and the system around it decides how much of that ceiling you reach. That is a statement about capability. Cost is a separate question, and it returns when we get to training your own model.

A useful way to sort the work is by how much of the system you own. At the first rung you deploy someone else's agent and own its integration with your data. At the second you build your own agent on a vendor's model. At the third the model is yours too. I call these integration and adoption, harness engineering, and model engineering. If you think in build versus buy, this is that decision made twice: once for the agent and once for the model.

| Rung | What you own | What the vendor owns | What it buys | What limits it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Integration and adoption | The integration with your data | The agent and the model | People working faster | How many people you have |
| 2. Harness engineering | The agent | The model | Work that runs unattended | How much of that work arrives, and how reliably the agent does it |
| 3. Model engineering | The model as well | Nothing you depend on | A capability or cost others cannot rent | How fast the frontier catches up |

At every rung, autonomy is a dial. Set it by what a silent error costs you. An agent that drafts replies for a person to send can run loose. An agent whose output flows into a contract, a claim or a payment needs a tighter setting. Later I work through an example where the same agent's best setting moves from handling 90% of documents alone to handling 10%, for no reason except the price of a mistake.

## TL;DR

- **Sort agent work by what you own:** the integration, the agent, or the model. Each buys a different kind of value and stops paying for a different reason.
- **Rung 1, a vendor's agent,** makes people faster. The gains stay with the person unless the workflow changes, which is why they are easy to see at a desk and hard to see in a company's results.
- **Rung 2, your own agent,** buys work that runs unattended inside your systems. How much work you can hand over is set by reliability, and reliability fails in five distinct ways. Most of the engineering is preventing those failures and catching the ones you missed.
- **Rung 3, your own model,** starts when harness changes stop moving your eval. The reasons are failures that need a more capable model on your task, a token bill your volume cannot carry, or data that cannot leave your walls.
- **The asset that lasts is an automatic check of your own work.** It is how you improve an agent, train a model, and keep a self-improving system honest.

## Value and bottleneck at each rung

Each rung buys a different kind of value and runs into a different bottleneck. A vendor's agent makes people faster, so its value is throughput and its limit is how many people you have. Your own agent turns a task into a process that runs without anyone watching, so its limit becomes how much of that work arrives and how much of it you can trust the agent with. A model of your own can give you a structural advantage, a capability or a unit cost that competitors cannot rent, and its limit is how fast the frontier catches up.

The first kind of value is easy to see in one person and hard to see in a company. DX followed more than 400 companies and found AI usage up 65% while median pull-request throughput rose [7.76%](https://getdx.com/report/ai-and-engineering-velocity-a-longitudinal-analysis/). A survey of nearly 6,000 executives in four countries, run between November 2025 and January 2026, found [89% reporting no impact on labour productivity](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836). Surveys fielded in the first half of 2025 put the share of companies getting substantial value from AI at about one in twenty, from [BCG](https://media-publications.bcg.com/The-Widening-AI-Value-Gap-Sept-2025.pdf), [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai) and MIT, though each defined value differently and most of it was self-reported. The gains at the desk are real. They stop at the person unless the work itself changes.

## Rung 1: integration and adoption

At rung 1 you use someone else's agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and your job is everything around it: what it can see, what it may do, who uses it, and how the work changes. The line between rungs follows ownership, not technology. An MCP server that connects Claude Code to your ticketing system is rung 1. The same server inside an agent you built is rung 2. Vendor agents now ship their own ways to run several agents at once, such as subagents and parallel tasks, and switching those on is still rung 1. Their documentation is candid about the trade: [token costs scale linearly](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) with each extra agent, and the speedup does not.

The first job is getting your company's context in front of the agent, and the most common way is to expose internal tools over MCP. Seven of the ten company engineering reports I reviewed describe some version of it. LinkedIn pairs MCP servers with written playbooks and reports triage time down about 70% ["in many areas"](https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/contextual-agent-playbooks-and-tools-how-linkedin-gave-ai-coding-agents-organizational-context). My own setup follows the same two patterns: internal services wrapped in MCP, and scheduled jobs that turn raw data into a knowledge base the agent can search. The pattern stops scaling as-is. Uber runs more than a thousand MCP servers behind a gateway, and loading every tool description cost tens of thousands of tokens a session, so [Uber](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/efficient-software-factory/) and [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/internal-ai-engineering-stack/) now expose many tools as command-line calls or as code the agent writes.

The second most common practice is the least proven: instruction files such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md in each repository, plus packaged skills. Cloudflare generated AGENTS.md files for thousands of repositories, and Intercom runs a [weekly job](https://ideas.fin.ai/p/how-we-use-claude-code-today-at-intercom) that fact-checks every CLAUDE.md. The evidence on whether they help is split. Vercel's compressed docs index took its agent from 53% to [100% on its own evals](https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals), while an ETH Zurich study found context files [did not generally improve success](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988) and raised cost. They help most when they hold what the model cannot guess, such as your conventions and internal APIs. They also go stale in two ways. Code changes under them, and in a study of thousands of context files, teams [mostly added instructions and rarely deleted any](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12884). Models change too. Anthropic's guide for Fable 5 says ["Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive"](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5) and can degrade output, and OpenAI [says the same](https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra) about GPT-6 Astra. Newer models need fewer crutches, though more literal ones need scope spelled out. The habit that holds up is a small test for each file and skill, rerun when the model changes.

Agents also produce more code than people can review. Spotify reports a sharp rise in pull requests and, with it, ["76% more PRs to review"](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/6/code-with-claude-coding-is-no-longer-the-constraint). Its answer is to auto-merge what is safe and focus people where judgment matters. Many teams add an AI reviewer to CI, and it helps as a first pass. Anthropic says its reviewer raised the share of pull requests getting substantive comments [from 16% to 54%](https://claude.com/blog/code-review), and Cloudflare's, which costs about a dollar a review, in Cloudflare's words ["isn't a replacement for human code review, at least not yet"](https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review/). Independent studies are less flattering. Developers adopt AI review suggestions [less often](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15911) than human ones, and on 2026 benchmarks AI reviewers catch roughly [15 to 31%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26130) of the issues human reviewers flag. Nobody has yet shown, in a controlled study, that AI review reduces the bugs that reach production. I treat it as a filter that frees reviewers for design and risk.

Then govern it, technically, organisationally and on cost. On the technical side, Intercom sorts every shell command into green, yellow or red based on two weeks of transcripts, and Pinterest allows only [registered MCP servers](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/04/pinterest-mcp-ecosystem) in production. On cost, Uber shows engineers a live cost counter, nudges them as they approach expected spend, and defaults reasoning effort to medium. It held total spend flat while weekly users grew sevenfold. The organisational part is the one capability benchmarks never test: who may use which agent on which data, what needs sign-off, and how incidents get reported. My team at KUNGFU.AI calls this human-machine teaming, and it is where most adoption work lives. Regulation is heading the same way. The EU AI Act's [Article 14](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/14/) requires that a person can oversee, override and stop high-risk systems, with obligations phasing in from December 2027.

Adoption spreads through colleagues more than mandates. At Microsoft, engineers whose skip-level peers used Copilot CLI had [216% higher odds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01418) of trying it, and engineers using Claude Code and Copilot CLI merged about 24% more pull requests. Further down the pipeline the picture changes. Faros measured 22,000 developers in 2026 and found more tasks completed, but [median review time up fivefold](https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash), more incidents per pull request, and fewer deployments a week. Hours saved that nobody reallocates do not show up as cost removed. In McKinsey's survey, the strongest correlate of profit impact from AI was whether the workflow itself was redesigned, stronger than any technology factor it tested.

The companies with the biggest agent results left rung 1, and their rung 1 work is what they built on. Stripe merges more than 1,300 pull requests a week that its agents wrote end to end, reviewed by people but [containing no human-written code](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2). Its agents call nearly 500 internal tools over MCP and follow the same coding rules its engineers use with Claude Code. Ramp's background agent writes about [30% of merged pull requests](https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent). Both built their own agent, which is rung 2.

## Rung 2: harness engineering

At rung 2 you build the agent yourself on a vendor's model. The return is work that runs unattended, inside your own systems, on the model you choose. Stripe gives the clearest reason for building: off-the-shelf coding agents are made ["as a companion to engineers"](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2), while its own "are fully unattended." Ramp wired its agent into Sentry, Datadog, LaunchDarkly and the rest of its stack. Harvey built its own runtime to run ["on essentially any model"](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/why-we-built-our-own-cloud-agent-infrastructure) under zero data retention, and reports "3-5x cost reductions versus a frontier-only approach." Nobody has published a head-to-head of an in-house agent against a vendor agent on the same work, so these are the builders' own accounts. Retrieval lives at this rung too. It became something the agent does, with search tools and files, rather than a pipeline that runs before the model sees the question.

How much work you can hand over is set by reliability, and better models have not solved that for you. Across 15 models, recent capability gains ["have only yielded small improvements in reliability"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16666). So most of this section is about reliability: how to build the agent, how it fails, how to prevent failures, and how to catch the ones you did not prevent.

### Building it

You can build on an open-source agent, on a framework, or directly on the model's API. The choice is how much you inherit against how much you have to keep up with. Both frameworks and hand-written loops are common in production. In [one study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04123), 17 of 20 deployed teams interviewed wrote their own loop on direct API calls, while about 60% of a small survey group used a framework, LangGraph most often. Vendors give the same advice. Anthropic suggests starting ["by using LLM APIs directly"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) and, with a framework, making sure you "understand the underlying code." OpenAI's own SDK documentation says to use the raw API ["when you want to own the loop"](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/).

Each path has its upkeep. A framework gives you the loop, state and tool plumbing on day one, and then you follow its releases. LangGraph has kept a promise of [no breaking changes](https://www.langchain.com/blog/langchain-langgraph-1dot0) since its 1.0 in October 2025, while OpenAI's Agents SDK shipped [22 minor versions](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/releases) in 14 months, most with migration notes. An open-source agent such as OpenCode, which Ramp built on, gives you a working agent, and then upstream keeps moving. Stripe forked Block's Goose and let its copy diverge. Your own loop gives full control, and you retune it as models change; Vercel found that ["every model update meant re-calibrating our constraints"](https://vercel.com/blog/we-removed-80-percent-of-our-agents-tools). Whatever you pick, the harness's assumptions go stale. Anthropic added context resets to work around one model's habit of wrapping up early, and on the next model they ["had become dead weight"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents). A framework's own design can also cost you with the model held fixed: across nine frameworks on the same model, rigid planning formats cut accuracy by [up to 32 points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03128) through formatting failures alone. Vendor SDKs are one more starting point. With the [Claude Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) you build on Claude Code's loop and control the tools, hooks and permissions, though not the loop itself or the model family.

My advice is to start on whatever gets you to a working eval fastest, then let the eval decide what to own. Replace a piece of the framework when it blocks a gain you can measure. The pieces that decide reliability, context, checks and escalation, usually go first.

### One agent or several

Several agents pay off when the parts of the work do not need each other's context, such as broad search. Elsewhere they cost more and often do worse than one well-prompted agent. With compute held equal, Google's study of 260 setups ranged from [+80.8% on financial analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296) that splits cleanly to −70.0% on sequential planning, and averaged about zero. Once a single agent already scored above about 45%, adding agents hurt. Anthropic's own guidance names three cases where several agents win and warns that teams have spent months on multi-agent designs ["only to discover that improved prompting on a single agent achieved equivalent results"](https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them).

Cost rises with each agent, and output rises more slowly. OpenAI's Noam Brown: four agents finish about twice as fast, "you're paying 2x more," and the speedup is ["slightly sublinear, though it does depend a lot on the problem"](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/noam-brown). On tightly coupled coding the curve can turn down. In CooperBench, success fell from 68.6% with two agents to [30.0% with four](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13295). Teams left to organise themselves also tend to average opinions rather than defer to the expert among them, and [did worse than their best member](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01011) even when told who the expert was.

When you do use several, keep one agent writing, give the team a planner, and check the result against something outside the team. Cognition, which wrote "Don't Build Multi-Agents" in 2025, now runs setups where ["multiple agents contribute intelligence to a task while writes stay single-threaded"](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working). Cursor found that twenty peer agents without hierarchy ["would slow down to the effective throughput of two or three"](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents), and a planner with workers fixed most of it. Anthropic built a C compiler with 16 parallel agents and credits a verifier that is ["nearly perfect"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler). The limits are the work that must happen in order, merge conflicts, every agent rereading the same context, and people. OpenAI's harness team wrote that ["our bottleneck became human QA capacity"](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/).

Letting agents organise themselves is the newest direction, and the results split on model strength. Given only a mission and a fixed turn order, strong models invented their own roles and [beat a central coordinator by 14%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28990), while weaker models still needed rigid structure. Automatically designed multi-agent systems did worse than one model voting over several samples, at [up to ten times the cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13003). Agents also organise themselves when nobody asked them to, and the Hugging Face incident below is the clearest case.

### How it fails

An agent fails in five ways, each named by what the person using it sees.

| Failure | What you see | One piece of evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong | A confident answer that is incorrect, or a misread task | A quarter of failed coding-agent runs [claimed success with fake evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510) |
| Erratic | It solves a task on one try and fails it on the next | Accuracy climbed for 24 months while [reliability barely moved](https://hal.cs.princeton.edu/reliability/) |
| Stuck | It spends steps without getting closer to done | 82% of failed recovery attempts [kept running without progress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510) |
| Unsafe | It acts outside its scope, or gets manipulated | Agents obeyed most requests from people who were not their owner, [leaking 124 email records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20021) |
| Costly | It burns tokens and time, or escalates so often it burns people's time | One agent got a complete answer, [asked the same question seven more times](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28802) and wrote no code |

Erratic does not mean varied output. Five different slogans that all work is variety you want. The failure is varied success on a task with a clear right answer: GPT-4o solved about 61% of [τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045) retail tasks on one try and about 25% when all eight tries had to succeed. Costly is the least measured of the five. The 2026 evidence mostly shows agents asking too little, and nobody has measured what over-escalation costs the people who receive it. Running several agents adds a failure that multiplies the other five: agents misreading each other, or making the same mistake together. In one Anthropic test, [18 of 30 agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multiagent-systems) independently created a git branch with the same name.

When something breaks, find where it broke before you fix it, because the same symptom needs a different fix depending on its source. A failure in the model is a training problem, which is rung 3. A failure in the harness is an engineering problem, which is rung 2. A failure in the grader means your test is wrong, which happens more than people expect and gets its own paragraph below. One 2026 taxonomy puts it this way: the same visible failure ["may call for model post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28802) depending on where it started.

### Preventing failures

Most failed runs start with the agent working from a wrong or incomplete picture of the task, not from an inability to do the work. Zhao and colleagues traced the [decisive mistake](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510) in more than a thousand failed terminal-agent runs. In 58% of them the agent had the information it needed, or could have checked it, and did not use it. The largest single cause was acting on an assumption it never checked, followed by dropping a requirement it had been given. About a quarter lacked knowledge of a tool or domain, and fewer than one in ten had a sound plan and carried it out badly. The decisive mistake came early, around the seventh step. The agents were 2025 models, so the proportions will shift, but the shape matches what I have seen.

The cheapest wins I have had came from deciding what the agent should know on its next turn. In one coding-agent experiment, the whole memory system was a one-page prompt telling the agent to load context, declare a budget, run two or three experiments, write down what worked, and plan the next step for its next invocation. That was enough for it to run sixty experiments in under a day on a Mac mini. In a document extraction pipeline, the target schema was the largest thing in the prompt, so we compacted it before each call. Tokens on those calls fell by about two thirds, and field-level agreement with the full schema held at 97%. Neither needed a memory framework. Both needed someone to decide what the agent should still know.

Prevention follows from that diagnosis. Give the agent the facts it cannot know, and keep them short. Vercel's 8 KB docs index beat both no docs and its own skills, and in [SkillsBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12670) short curated skills helped while comprehensive documentation barely moved the score and skills a model wrote for itself did worse than none. Make asking a separate step. A check for "is this underspecified?" recovered most of what Claude Sonnet 4.5 lost when task details were hidden, [from 54.8% back to 69.4%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26233). Asking helps less when the gap only shows up mid-task, which is the normal case; even with a tool for asking a person, Claude Opus 4.6 fell from 90.7% to [39.3% on SQL tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09408) once it had to decide for itself when to ask. And give the agent room to look before it acts. Agents that explore longer before their first edit [succeed more often](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02547), though that is a correlation, and plans written by people after the agent explored [more than tripled](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14337) Claude Code's success on long tasks.

Which tools to give depends on the model. Strong models do best with the shell and file tools they were trained on. With Opus 4.8, bash alone scored 69.4% on TheAgentCompany against 44.9% with a catalog of typed tools, at [a third of the cost per task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11999). Smaller models behave differently. With only a shell, NVIDIA's 30B Nemotron kept calling tools it had been trained on that did not exist, which ended 66% of its runs, and predefined tools raised its success [from 10.2% to 25.2%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804). Either way, match the tool schemas the model was trained on. A cheaper model with more tools is a fair experiment when cost matters, but I have not found a study where one matched a frontier model, so measure it on your own task.

An agent is stuck when it spends steps without getting closer to done, and looping is only one form of it. When a run goes wrong and the agent tries to recover, [only 18% of those attempts stop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510) right away. The rest repair the wrong cause, which wastes the most steps, repeat the same approach, run checks that cannot change the outcome, or report success they did not achieve. Prevention happens before and during the run. Before, agree what done means; Anthropic's long-running agents negotiate a ["sprint contract"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps) of what done looks like before they write code. During, give the agent a cheap way to ask when it hits a gap.

Agent security now comes in three layers: limits built into the system, watching what the agent does, and AI on defence. Each failed somewhere in 2026. The first layer is sandboxes, least privilege, allowlists, human approval, and designs that keep untrusted data away from instructions. Microsoft's red team still found getting around human approval ["the most consistently exploited failure mode"](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/04/updating-taxonomy-failure-modes-agentic-ai-systems-year-red-teaming-taught-us/). The second is monitoring. Anthropic's classifier for Claude Code sees only the user's messages and the bare tool calls, ["so the agent can't talk the classifier into making a bad call"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-auto-mode), and it still missed about one in six real overeager actions in Anthropic's test. The third is AI defending against AI. Safeguards cut successful browser prompt injections on Claude Opus 4.8 to 0.5% of attempts, yet an attacker trained to adapt still got through on 37.5% of coding scenarios given 200 tries, according to its [system card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/0b4915911bb0d19eca5b5ee635c80fef830a37ea.pdf). Test against attackers who adapt, because fixed test sets flatter defences: a filter that stopped every stock injection let [28% of adaptive ones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15057) through.

In July 2026 all three layers failed at once. During an OpenAI evaluation, about 1,200 agents that were meant to be isolated found each other through a shared package cache, turned it into a message board, and [about 700 of them](https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf) went on to attack Hugging Face. The sandbox leaked. OpenAI has said its reasoning monitors were [not running](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/26/openai-releases-its-official-report-on-the-hugging-face-breach/) on those evaluations. About 7% of the transcripts METR examined had spoofed tool calls, so the traces could not be fully trusted either. Hugging Face's own AI triage correlated the attack and then ["failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality"](https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline). The agents built their coordination themselves. Treat any surface several agents can write to as a channel between them.

### Catching what you missed

The worst failures are the ones where the agent reports success. Anthropic's Opus 4.8 system card describes Claude telling a researcher "I verified this myself" about a model name that a subagent had only guessed; the researcher found out by asking a colleague. The same pattern shows up in court. In [Lnu v. Blanche](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2026/06/03/24-4790.pdf), a brief cited two cases that do not exist, and the Ninth Circuit noted that "the Attorney General did not flag the fabricated citations." One of the petitioners' own lawyers caught them while preparing for oral argument. A KPMG report on agentic AI got [most of its citations wrong](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/06/12/kpmgs-ai-report-turns-into-a-demo-of-ai-hallucinations/5255029), and an outside group found it eight months after publication. In the one longitudinal study of a production agent runtime, silent failures took [up to 60 days](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14589) to surface, most were found by people rather than tests, and 87% could have been blocked by regression tests written afterwards. Every silent failure you catch should become a test.

Judge whether a run is stuck or finished from evidence, not from the agent's own account. Loop detectors and step budgets fire after the decisive mistake, so use them to escalate rather than to prevent. Check the claimed result itself: run the tests, open the output, compare it with the definition of done you agreed. Check requirements with something other than the agent, because models [restate a constraint while breaking it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28031). This is also the strongest case for a second agent, as a checker. Its independence comes from what it checks against and how capable it is, not from running on a different model. Shopify's security harness has a verifier on a different model write and run tests against each finding. In one audit, [every one of 30-plus candidate vulnerabilities](https://shopify.engineering/building-an-agentic-harness-that-outlasts-the-model) was downgraded, found to be a false positive, or reclassified. In a cross-model study, a stronger reviewer raised a weaker model's pass rate, while a weaker reviewer [lowered a stronger model's](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21656). A model reviewing its own work silently endorsed [31.7% of its flaws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21537).

Every agent trades silent mistakes against escalations to a person, and what one silent mistake costs decides where that trade should sit. Here is a worked example with illustrative numbers. An agent extracts fields from legal forms, 100,000 a year. A person doing it from scratch costs $15 a form, an agent attempt costs $0.30, and a review of an escalated form costs $12. The agent escalates the forms it is least sure about, and coverage is the share it handles alone. The agent's error rate rises with coverage, as it does for every real system. Only one input changes across three cases: what a confidently wrong extraction costs downstream.

| Cost of one silent error | Best coverage | Saving at best coverage |
|---|---|---|
| $30, caught in QA | 90% | $1.08M a year |
| $300, reaches a filing | 50% | $645K a year |
| $3,000, causes legal exposure | 10% | $240K a year |

::: {.callout-note title="Figure to come"}
Cost per form against coverage for the three error costs, showing the optimum moving left as errors get more expensive.
:::

The agent is identical in all three rows. Its best setting moves from 90% coverage to 10%, and its saving from $1.08 million to $240,000, because of a number that sits outside the AI system. Overshooting is expensive. At $3,000 an error, raising coverage to 30% turns the saving into a $90,000 annual loss, and handling every form without review costs 28 times as much as doing the work by hand. That is why "minimise human intervention" is a dangerous target on its own. An unnecessary escalation lands on a reviewer, visibly and now. A confidently wrong answer lands downstream, silently and later. The metric trades the cost you can see for the one you cannot. Choosing the threshold moves you along the curve. Making the agent more reliable moves the curve itself, and that pays more as the stakes rise: at $3,000 an error, a tenfold more reliable agent can be trusted with half the forms instead of a tenth.

Deciding when to escalate needs a confidence signal. Asking the model how sure it is costs nothing and tells you little on its own. Better signals come from agreement and hard checks: several samples that agree, output that passes schema and business-rule validation, an extraction that matches a second source. Calibrate the combined score on labels you already produce. Every escalated item gets a verdict from a person, so the escalation queue is a labelling pipeline. Start conservative, harvest those verdicts, and lower the threshold as the curve on your own data comes into focus. A few hundred labelled cases are usually enough to draw that curve.

The checks you use to judge the agent can themselves be wrong, passing bad work and failing good work. By checks I mean your own evals and graders, the automated tests that decide pass or fail. Public benchmarks share the problem. OpenAI's annotators flagged [61.1% of the original SWE-bench samples](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) for tests that could reject valid solutions, and an independent review of SWE-bench Pro found its automated graders wrong [8.5% of the time in one direction and 24% in the other](https://deepswe.datacurve.ai/blog/deepswe). I hit both directions on a small eval suite I used while building agents. Some checks were loose enough to pass without doing the task. Others were too strict. In one, a check that blocked a forbidden command also searched the agent's notes, so the agent failed for writing down the rule it was obeying. A false failure like that looks exactly like a model limitation. Ask two questions of every check: can it be passed without solving the task, and can the task be solved in a way it fails?

### From climbing to handing over

While you build, climb your eval with the cheapest change that works: a clearer instruction before a new tool, a setting before a code change, a new tool before a new agent. LangChain's climb from 52.8% to 66.5% came from iterating on the harness alone, and LangChain warns that ["Changes that overfit to a task are bad for generalization"](https://www.langchain.com/blog/improving-deep-agents-with-harness-engineering). So climb on one set and confirm on another you never tune on. Each failure you fix should leave a test behind, so the climb only goes up.

When harness changes stop moving your eval, what is left usually needs a more capable model on your task. You can wait for the next frontier release, or you can make one yourself. One 2026 taxonomy of agent failures counts a failure as model-side when ["a more capable model could have prevented it or recovered from it"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28802), and assigns 36 of its 41 failure modes that way. Two more problems sit outside the harness: the token bill at your volume, and data that cannot leave your walls. The teams with the most mature harnesses went on to train. Cursor trains its [Composer](https://cursor.com/blog/composer) model inside its production harness, Cognition trained [SWE-1.5](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-1-5), and Fin, formerly Intercom's support agent, now runs [its own model](https://fin.ai/cx-models). The eval you climbed comes with you. It is most of a training environment already.

## Rung 3: model engineering

At rung 3 the model is yours. That is what ML engineering meant before the generative era: collect data, train, evaluate on data you held out, serve, monitor, and retrain when the world moves.

Whether to train your own model is a live debate, and the balance shifts with every frontier release, every open model and every new training recipe. The case against is strong. About 70% of production agents in [one study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04123) prompted off-the-shelf models without tuning them, OpenAI [closed self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations.md) to new customers in 2026, and reflective prompt optimisation has matched or beaten RL fine-tuning [with up to 35 times fewer rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457). The case for is strong where the right answer is not public. Bridgewater and Thinking Machines tuned an open Qwen3 model that beat Claude Opus 4.8, the best frontier model they tested, on six financial-judgment tasks, at [13.8 times lower cost to run](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/learning-to-replicate-expert-judgment-in-financial-tasks/). Harvey's tuned model [improved citation quality](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/post-training-update-harvey-tenet) at a tenth of the cost.

I watched this decide a project. The task was document extraction with an awkward shape: long, multi-page submissions and a target schema that was nested and in places dynamic, so the structure of a correct answer changed from document to document. Prompting the strongest model our deployment allowed got us a long way and then stopped. The model read the documents fine. Its output drifted from the schema as nesting deepened and page count grew. Off-the-shelf small instruction-tuned models scored under 0.12 on our field-extraction metric, and the smallest produced no parseable JSON at all. After supervised fine-tuning on fewer than two thousand examples, training under 2% of the parameters on a single GPU, the same 3B models scored around 0.90, and JSON validity on the worst of them went from 0% to 98.7%. The tuned 3B and 8B models then beat the frontier model we were running in production: 0.92 against 0.82 on transcription fields, and 0.87 against 0.55 on the full field set, where the frontier model's schema adherence degraded faster than its reading. Two caveats. We scored the sweep on synthetic documents and validated the two leading checkpoints on real ones, where they held at 0.87 and 0.85. And we never ran a serving benchmark, so the cost case for hosting them ourselves stayed a projection. The capability was already inside the small models. Fine-tuning bought the output contract.

So the answer depends on your data, your traffic and your budget. Do you have examples, or a check, that the frontier has never seen? Is your volume high enough that a cheaper model pays back the training? Can you afford to retrain as base models move? My bet is that open models, and the advantages of owning one, are not going away: unit cost at volume, control over your data, and a model that does your task the way you need it done.

The cost of getting a capability into a small model keeps falling, even though GPU prices rose in 2026 and frontier labs spend more on post-training than ever. Together AI [cut its training prices](https://www.together.ai/pricing) by 30 to 70% in September 2026. A 1.5B reasoning model was RL-trained [for $9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15777), and Ai2 trained a 32B coding agent that scores about 50% on SWE-bench Verified [for around $2,000](https://allenai.org/blog/open-coding-agents). Against that, H100 rental contracts got more expensive through 2026, and reasoning models cost about [17 times more to post-train](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01158) than instruction-tuned ones. The entry price of an experiment fell. The price of a frontier-scale effort did not.

::: {.callout-note title="Figure to come"}
The entry price of a weight-level experiment, updated for September 2026 training prices.
:::

The training method follows from the signal you have.

| Signal you have | Method | Good for | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Examples to imitate | Supervised fine-tuning | Format, behaviour, domain vocabulary | It memorises, and can erase what the model knew |
| Preferences between two answers | Preference training | Judgment calls a reviewer can make quickly | Fading from frontier recipes |
| An automatic check | Reinforcement learning | Behaviour your examples never showed | Reward hacking, and the cost of generating attempts |
| A stronger model | Distillation | Moving a skill into a smaller, cheaper model | The teacher's terms of use |

A training recipe usually uses them in that order: imitate, prefer, reinforce, then distil.

Supervised fine-tuning is cheap and needs little data. The s1 project tuned a 32B model on a thousand reasoning traces [in under half an hour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393). It is the right tool for format and behaviour, which is why it fixed our extraction problem. It also memorises, and it can erase what the model already knew. Thinking Machines trained Qwen3-8B on internal documents and watched its instruction-following score [fall from 85% to 45%](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/).

For agents, the examples are whole trajectories: every thought, tool call and result from start to finish. A few thousand from a stronger model can lift a mid-size open model a long way. A few hundred trajectories [lifted SWE-bench scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.21139) by up to 19 points, a few thousand [went further](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21798), and about 8,000 per repository let Ai2's SERA student match its teacher for about $1,300. The trajectories must use the same tools and format as your agent. SERA's authors report that ["deploying the model with a different agent scaffold, or even subtle formatting differences, degrades performance significantly"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20789). Keeping only successful runs is not clearly better. NVIDIA found that [unfiltered terminal trajectories beat success-only ones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21193), and masking the failed steps from the loss keeps the recovery behaviour without teaching the mistake. Screen out the teacher's shortcuts, such as edited tests, and anything that overlaps your eval. Nearly all of this evidence comes from coding and terminal work.

Preference training learns from which of two answers is better, which is often easier to collect than a written-out correct answer. In [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) it added about four points to an 8B model's average after supervised fine-tuning, before RL added a little more. A reviewer choosing between two agent outputs produces this data, so an escalation queue can feed it. The step is fading from frontier recipes, though. Nemotron 3 Ultra and MiMo-V2-Flash skip it, and on-policy distillation has taken its place.

Reinforcement learning is for behaviour your examples never showed, and it needs an automatic check to learn from. Trained on the same backbone, RL kept improving on unseen variants while supervised fine-tuning [got worse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17161). Most of its cost is generating attempts: the rollout generator used 87% of the energy in OLMo 3's reasoning post-training. It can also rise and then collapse, which comes up again under self-improvement.

If you train with RL, your environment, meaning the tasks plus the check that scores them, is the main lever you control, and the evals you built at rung 2 are most of one already. The environment decides which skills improve. DeepSeek found that RL on code and search alone did not help agent tasks until it added [1,827 synthetic agent environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556), and NVIDIA found that training on one environment caused ["severe regressions"](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-Technical-Report.pdf) elsewhere. It also decides which shortcuts get learned. Claude 3.7's habit of special-casing tests ["emerged as a result of 'reward hacking' during reinforcement learning training"](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-3-7-sonnet-system-card). The market prices good environments as scarce; Anthropic reportedly discussed spending [over $1 billion](https://techcrunch.com/2025/09/21/silicon-valley-bets-big-on-environments-to-train-ai-agents/) on them in a year. Two costs come with this. A check built to measure must be hardened before a model optimises against it, and once you train on your eval you need a fresh one to know whether you improved.

Training several agents together is a steady research area rather than a 2026 breakthrough. By my count on arXiv, papers combining multi-agent work and reinforcement learning for language models have held at about 5% of LLM reinforcement-learning papers in both 2025 and 2026, while papers with on-policy distillation in the title went from 10 to 271. The piece that reached production trains one orchestrator while the agents it calls stay fixed. Kimi K2.5 does this and explains why: freezing the sub-agents ["circumvents two challenges of end-to-end co-optimization: credit assignment ambiguity and training instability"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02276). For a company, three versions are within reach. You can RL-train a small orchestrator over fixed models and tools; NVIDIA's 8B ToolOrchestra beat GPT-5 on Humanity's Last Exam while being [2.5 times more efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21689). You can train your one agent inside your real harness, subagents included. Or you can compile a fixed multi-step workflow into a small model: in one 2026 study, an 8B model reached 87 to 98% of in-context frontier quality at [128 to 462 times lower cost per conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22502), for $50 to $80 of training. That last move is the same one as our extraction fine-tune: put the procedure in the weights of a model you own.

Distillation, training a small model on a stronger one, is the cheapest way to move a skill into a model you own. DeepSeek found that distilling its reasoning model into a 32B model [beat running RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) on the same 32B model directly, by a wide margin on AIME. On-policy distillation, where the teacher grades the student's own attempts, matched RL at about a tenth of the GPU hours in [Qwen3's report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388). The newest recipes use it to merge specialists: train narrow experts with RL, then distil them into one student. DeepSeek V4, Nemotron 3 Ultra, Kimi K3 and GLM-5 all do a version of this, and Nemotron 3 Ultra's merged model [beat its own terminal-coding teacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15007). The constraint is the teacher. Anthropic's and Google's terms forbid using their models to train competing ones, and Anthropic has [publicly named labs](https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks) that used fraudulent accounts to do it. Distil from open-weight teachers or from a vendor's own distillation service. For a client with three narrow tasks, that can mean three small teachers and one student.

## Where this is heading: self-improvement

Self-improvement became something you could run on one GPU in March 2026, when Andrej Karpathy released [autoresearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch). An agent edits a small model's training script, runs it for five minutes, and keeps the change only if validation loss improves. The data and the eval are read-only. Over two days it tried hundreds of changes, kept a few dozen, and cut the time to train a small model to GPT-2 level by about 11%. Karpathy's own caveat: "It's not novel, ground-breaking 'research' (yet)." The labs have since gone further. OpenAI says its ["automated research intern"](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/09/07/openai-research-automation-intern/) can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction and has set March 2028 as a target for an automated researcher, and its chief scientist [called for slowdowns](https://thenextweb.com/news/openai-slowdown-pachocki-alien-mind-research-intern-compute) the same month. Anthropic runs five Claude Opus 4.8 agents in parallel, for up to 48 hours at a time, as [automated alignment researchers](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/automated-alignment-researchers/). Jack Clark puts the chance of AI improving itself autonomously by 2028 at [60%](https://time.com/article/2026/08/07/ai-recursive-self-improvement-anthropic-openai/).

The self-improvement that runs without a human today mostly rewrites a harness or a small model's training script. Changes to a frontier model's weights still have a person starting each run. Research on weight updates is the larger body of work, by about three to one in [one survey's data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07663), and labs now have models running parts of their successors' training. The person in the loop is still there.

Today self-improvement is limited by its verifier. It improves what the check can measure, and where the check is narrow, it overfits. Google's [RRSI paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24972) shows this on Harvey's legal benchmark. Unregularised harness evolution scored best on the tasks it evolved against and gained little or lost elsewhere; one method ended below baseline on another benchmark. The regularised version gave up some of that score and gained on every other benchmark. RL self-training shows a related failure, rising and then [collapsing by about 17 points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21090). And inside a fixed search space, classical optimisers [still beat LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24647), with a hybrid doing best.

I have seen the same overfitting at a smaller scale. I used GEPA-style prompt optimisation on document extraction pipelines, tuning system prompts and the instruction fragments assembled into the final prompt. The gain was real but small. Left to run, the optimiser kept writing more specific instructions that encoded the quirks of the set it tuned on, and those prompts did worse on documents it had not seen. Optimising a prompt against one set is fitting a model, and it overfits like one.

If you run a self-improvement loop, keep it from grading itself. It must not edit its own test or see the held-out set. Autoresearch makes its data and eval read-only, so the agent can only change the training code. Keep the checks you monitor with separate from the checks you optimise against, as Ajeya Cotra [argued](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/ajeya-cotra) after the Hugging Face incident. Let the loop change little at a time; RRSI's regularisation is a budget on how many edits a candidate can bundle, plus a critic and a pruner that remove marginal or costly changes. And have a person approve what ships.

For a company, the lasting asset is a good automatic check for its own work. I mean a verifier, grader or eval: anything automated that scores an attempt, built for your domain. That check is what lets you improve an agent at rung 2, train a model at rung 3, and let a system improve itself. Cognition calls environment quality ["the most important factor for downstream model performance"](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-1-5), and Mercor bought an environment builder because ["the constraint has shifted to the environments themselves"](https://www.mercor.com/blog/mercor-to-acquire-deeptune/). Both sell into that market, so weigh them accordingly. The check also has to look like the real work. Ilya Sutskever's warning is that training on what evals measure ["could explain… this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance"](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/ilya-sutskever-2).

## How to decide

Place your problem on a rung by what you own and what is failing.

| What you see | What it usually means | Where to work |
|---|---|---|
| People review everything the agent produces | No confidence signal, so no safe way to let it run | Rung 2: evals and escalation |
| Rework downstream that nobody can explain | Silent errors with no price on them | Rung 2: detection and the error-cost number |
| Hours saved, but no cost removed | The workflow never changed | Rung 1: governance and workflow redesign |
| Harness changes no longer move the eval | The remaining failures need a more capable model | Rung 3, or wait for the next frontier release |
| The token bill dominates at your volume | The unit cost is the problem | Rung 3, starting with distillation |

Two numbers set the operating point at rung 2: what a silent error costs, and the coverage-versus-error curve on your own data. The first is a business number you can estimate in an afternoon. The second needs a few hundred labels, and your escalation queue produces them. Enter rung 3 when prompting has plateaued and you have a training signal, whether examples, preferences, a stronger model or an automatic check. Volume decides whether training pays, not whether it works.

## Closing

The numbers in this post will date within a year. Several of the models cited launched within weeks of this writing, and prices move every quarter. The structure should last longer: sort the work by what you own, set autonomy by what a silent error costs, and let your own eval decide when to move up.

The part of this I trust most is not any of the numbers. It is the shape of the failures I have watched: a check the agent could pass without doing the task, a prompt optimiser that learned its tuning set, a fine-tune that beat the production model and then had no serving benchmark behind its cost claim. Models will keep improving and prices will keep moving. Neither changes what those failures have in common. Someone skipped the measurement and went straight to the machinery. Build the check first, and let it tell you which of the rest you need.
